agentCan: Drive the App Console form-filling (scopes, redirect URIs, branding) given account access
Implement the full OAuth flow with PKCE or secret, short-lived token handling, and offline refresh
Draft the production application (API-use description, least-privilege justification)

approval.cost: No fee mentioned in the docs (unstated)
approval.trigger: Production status approval, required for unlimited users. Mechanics: in development status you may link up to 500 users total, but once you link 50 users a two-week clock starts: apply for AND receive production approval within it or linking freezes (unlinking users does not unfreeze). Dropbox will not even review the application until you reach 50 linked users, unless an early-review exception is granted. Review checks branding-guideline and terms compliance plus least-privilege fit.
approval.wait: Not stated. Dropbox publishes no review duration or SLA; only your two-week deadline is specified

blockers.detail: Your pilot can strand at user 51: at 50 linked users you have two weeks to be production-approved or the app stops linking new users, and the only cure is approval itself. Meanwhile Dropbox won't review you before 50 users. Plan the application before you need it, or request early review with evidence.
blockers.howToClear: Write the production application early, be descriptive (Dropbox says detail speeds approval), and use the early-review field if your launch cannot wait for 50 organic users.
blockers.title: The 50-user / two-week freeze trap

blockers.detail: App folder (a dedicated folder under /Apps) vs Full Dropbox (everything, within scopes) is chosen at creation. Changing it requires deleting the app and creating a new one: new app key, every user re-links. Production review also polices this choice: requesting Full Dropbox when an app folder would do can sink approval.
blockers.howToClear: Decide from your real data needs: agents touching only their own content should take App folder; pre-existing user files anywhere require Full Dropbox.
blockers.title: Access type is a one-way door

blockers.detail: Adding any team scope (Team Info, Membership, Event log, etc.) makes the token belong to the whole team: only a team admin can authorize, individual accounts hit a dead end, and member actions go through Dropbox-API-Select-User.
blockers.howToClear: Request individual scopes only unless you are deliberately building a team-admin product.
blockers.title: Team scopes change the whole trust model

tested: Read-only verification: app creation wizard, scope model, development/production status mechanics, and the freeze rules were checked against current dropbox.com/developers and docs.dropboxapi.com pages (no app created, nothing submitted)
unverified: Production review duration or SLA: not published anywhere in the official pages read; only the developer's two-week deadline is stated.
Whether any production application fee exists (none mentioned).
Whether Chooser/Saver-only apps are exempt from the 500/50 mechanics in all cases (docs say components need no production approval).

alternatives: Pre-built components (Chooser/Saver/Embedder): no production approval needed, since the user grants access to specific files inside Dropbox's own UI
flavor.recommended: Scoped-access API app; App folder access unless you must touch pre-existing files anywhere
flavor.why: Modern Dropbox apps select individual OAuth scopes in the App Console instead of blanket permission types. The content-access decision (App folder vs Full Dropbox) is made at creation and is effectively permanent, so it is the first real product decision, before any code.

humanMust: Own the Dropbox account and make the App folder vs Full Dropbox call
Write and submit the production application before the two-week clock becomes a crisis
name: Dropbox
nuances: App name locks once production-approved; changes after that require contacting Dropbox.
Without token_access_type=offline on the authorize URL you get only a short-lived access token; long-lived tokens are deprecated. Re-auth is silent while the user's approval remains valid.
You can request a subset of your console-enabled scopes per authorization and step up later with re-authorization; over-asking both deters users and can hurt your production review.
A privacy policy is an explicit expectation for production readiness.
If you build a developer tool on top of Dropbox, your developers must register their own apps and keys; you cannot lend yours.
prerequisites: A Dropbox account (free is enough to start)
The App folder vs Full Dropbox decision (one-way door)
Your redirect URI and minimal scope list
Branding assets per the Dropbox Branding Guide (also used in production review)

steps.detail: App Console > Create app: choose Scoped access, then the access type (App folder recommended; Full Dropbox only if you must reach pre-existing files anywhere), name the app per the Branding Guide naming rules, Create app. A free account suffices.
steps.title: Create the app (choose access type carefully)

steps.detail: Settings tab shows the App key and App secret and Development status. Permissions tab: check only the individual scopes your app uses (endpoints document their required scope), then Submit. Fill the Branding tab (publisher, description, website, icons): users see it on the authorization page and reviewers use it later.
steps.title: Save credentials, select scopes, add branding

steps.detail: Settings > OAuth 2: register exact Redirect URIs (Dropbox matches the redirect_uri parameter against them). Disable the implicit grant if unused. A Generate button mints a test token for your own account so you can test before writing OAuth code.
steps.title: Register redirect URIs

steps.detail: Authorize at dropbox.com/oauth2/authorize (client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code; add token_access_type=offline if you need refresh tokens, which you almost always do). Exchange the code at /oauth2/token with the app secret, or use PKCE for clients that cannot keep a secret. Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens mint new ones.
steps.title: Implement the OAuth flow

steps.detail: Settings > Development users > Enable additional users. Up to 500 total users can link while in development status; demos and internal tools can stay here indefinitely. Watch your linked-user count: 50 is the tripwire.
steps.title: Enable additional users for your pilot

steps.detail: From the app page, Apply for Production with a detailed description of how your app uses the API and your icon uploaded. Dropbox reviews branding/terms compliance and least-privilege fit; denial comes with feedback and you can resubmit. Remember: review starts only at 50 linked users (or via the early-review field), and approval must land within two weeks of crossing 50.
steps.time: Application ~30 min; review duration not stated
steps.title: Apply for production before the clock hurts

tagline: Setup takes minutes and pilots can run to 500 users, but Dropbox hides a tripwire: at 50 linked users a two-week clock starts, and if production approval doesn't land in time, linking freezes.

time.active: ~30 min of console work + ~1 hr of OAuth coding
time.total: Same day to a 500-user pilot; unlimited public use waits on a production review whose duration Dropbox does not publish
time.waiting: Unstated (production review has no published SLA)
